dashboard.description: A Redis dashboard for monitoring Itential usage.

panels.description: This metric tracks how long the Redis instance has been running since its last start, measured in seconds. It's important because an uptime of zero indicates the instance has crashed or been stopped, meaning complete service unavailability. A zero uptime indicates catastrophic failure - the Redis process has died, was killed, or the server crashed. Resolution requires immediate investigation of Redis logs (`/var/log/redis/redis-server.log`), checking for OOM kills in system logs (`dmesg | grep -i kill`), verifying the server hasn't run out of memory or disk space, checking for configuration errors that prevent startup, and potentially restarting the Redis service while addressing the root cause. This is your most critical alert as it means complete data unavailability.
panels.title: Redis Uptime

panels.description: This metric measures the percentage of CPU time consumed by Redis processes (both main and child processes for RDB/AOF operations) over a 5-minute window. It's important because high CPU usage indicates Redis is working hard to process commands, perform persistence operations, or handle replication, which can lead to increased latency and degraded performance. Elevated CPU (>70%) suggests Redis is under heavy load from too many operations, expensive commands (like KEYS *), or background tasks like AOF rewrites and RDB snapshots competing for CPU. Resolution involves identifying expensive commands through `SLOWLOG GET`, optimizing application queries, reviewing if background persistence operations coincide with peak traffic (consider scheduling AOF rewrites during off-peak hours), checking for inefficient Lua scripts, ensuring proper indexing in your BullMQ job data structures, and potentially scaling horizontally by adding more Redis instances if the workload legitimately requires more CPU capacity.
panels.title: CPU Usage

panels.description: This metric tracks the total bytes of memory currently allocated by Redis for storing data, overhead, and buffers. It's critical because Redis is an in-memory database, and when memory is exhausted, Redis either starts evicting keys (data loss) or refuses new writes, causing application failures. High memory usage (>80%) indicates you're approaching the configured maxmemory limit, which triggers eviction policies and can cause data loss in your BullMQ jobs. Resolution requires analyzing memory usage with `MEMORY STATS` and `MEMORY DOCTOR`, identifying large keys with `redis-cli --bigkeys`, reviewing your BullMQ job retention policies to ensure completed/failed jobs are cleaned up, checking for memory leaks in job data, verifying TTLs are set appropriately on temporary data, considering increasing the maxmemory limit if you have physical RAM available, or implementing data archival strategies to move old jobs to persistent storage like PostgreSQL or MongoDB.
panels.title: Memory Usage

panels.description: This metric shows how many replica instances are currently connected to the master from the master's perspective. It's critical for data durability because replicas provide redundancy - if the master fails, Sentinel can promote a replica, but only if replicas exist and are synchronized. A count below your expected number (2 in our setup) indicates a replica has disconnected due to network issues, the replica process crashed, or replication was manually disabled. Resolution involves checking the replica's Redis logs for connection errors, verifying network connectivity between master and replica with telnet, ensuring firewall rules allow Redis replication traffic, checking if the replica is running with `systemctl status redis-server`, reviewing Sentinel logs for failover events that may have changed topology, verifying replication authentication passwords match, and investigating whether `min-replicas-to-write` is preventing writes (which is actually protecting you from data loss).
panels.title: Replicas

panels.description: This metric indicates whether a replica can successfully communicate with its master, showing 1 for connected and 0 for disconnected from the replica's perspective. It's critical because a broken master link means the replica is no longer receiving updates and is serving stale data, making it unsuitable for promotion during failover. A value of 0 indicates network partition between replica and master, master has crashed, incorrect master configuration on the replica, authentication failure, or firewall blocking replication traffic. Resolution requires checking replica logs for connection errors (`master_link_down_since_seconds`), verifying master is running and reachable, testing network connectivity with `redis-cli -h master-host PING`, checking authentication credentials match between master and replica using `CONFIG GET masterauth`, reviewing Redis configuration for correct master IP and port, ensuring replication backlog is large enough to avoid full resyncs, and investigating whether this is part of a planned failover or network maintenance.
panels.title: Primary Link

panels.description: This metric counts the number of client connections currently established to Redis, excluding connections from replicas. It's important because each connection consumes memory and file descriptors, and too many connections can indicate connection leaks or connection pooling issues in your applications. High client counts (>8000) suggest your BullMQ workers or Itential services are creating excessive connections rather than reusing them from a pool, you have a connection leak where connections aren't being closed, or you're experiencing a connection storm from application restarts. Resolution involves auditing your application code to ensure proper connection pooling (BullMQ should reuse connections), checking for client timeout settings that may keep idle connections open too long, using `CLIENT LIST` to identify which clients are connected and from which IPs, investigating whether recent deployments introduced connection leaks, configuring appropriate timeout values in Redis to close idle connections, and reviewing your BullMQ worker scaling - you may have too many workers relative to your workload.
panels.title: Active Clients

panels.description: This metric shows how many additional client connections Redis can accept before reaching the `maxclients` limit. It's important as a capacity planning metric and early warning system - running out of client slots means Redis will reject new connections, causing application failures. Low available slots indicate you're approaching the connection limit, which could cause "max number of clients reached" errors that will break your BullMQ job processing. Resolution involves increasing the `maxclients` configuration setting in redis.conf if you legitimately need more connections, but more importantly, investigating why you need so many connections - this usually indicates poor connection management in applications, so focus on implementing connection pooling, fixing connection leaks, ensuring BullMQ workers properly share connections, and reviewing whether you have too many worker processes running simultaneously.
panels.title: Available Client Slots

panels.description: This is a configuration setting that defines the maximum number of client connections Redis will accept. It's important as a capacity limit that prevents Redis from consuming all available file descriptors and system resources. The default is 10,000, which is usually sufficient, but in high-concurrency environments with many BullMQ workers, you might need to increase it. If you're hitting this limit, resolution involves increasing the value in redis.conf (`maxclients 20000`), but also increasing the system's file descriptor limit (`ulimit -n`) to accommodate more connections, and crucially, investigating whether the high connection count is necessary or indicates a connection pooling problem in your applications - fixing the root cause is better than just raising the limit.
panels.title: Max Clients

panels.description: The rate of CPU usage as reported by Redis includes the main, child, and totals.
panels.title: Total Redis CPU Usage

panels.title: Instance Info

panels.description: CPU stats broken down by user vs system.
panels.title: CPU Breakdown (User vs System)

panels.description: This panel displays the percentage of disk space currently used across all filesystems on the selected instance. The metric is calculated by determining the ratio of available space to total filesystem size, then subtracting from 100 to show usage rather than availability - providing an intuitive view where higher percentages indicate fuller disks. Each physical filesystem is displayed as a separate line, with virtual filesystems like rootfs excluded to focus on actual storage devices. Monitoring disk usage percentage is critical for preventing outages, as full disks can cause applications to crash, databases to fail, prevent log writes, and block normal system operations. This metric should be watched closely with alerts typically set at 85% (warning) and 95% (critical) thresholds, as different filesystems have different tolerances - for example, MongoDB data directories require immediate attention when approaching 95% full, as write operations can hang or fail. Regular monitoring allows for proactive capacity planning, identifying growth trends, and taking corrective action such as cleaning up old files, rotating logs, or expanding storage before reaching critical levels.
panels.title: Disk Space Used

panels.description: This panel displays the number of available inodes (file system entries) on each filesystem for the selected instance. Inodes are data structures that store information about files and directories - each file, directory, or symlink requires one inode. Even if disk space is available, running out of inodes prevents creation of new files. This metric monitors inode availability across all physical filesystems, excluding virtual filesystems like rootfs. Low inode counts can occur when many small files are created (such as logs, cache files, or email storage), and reaching zero available inodes will cause "No space left on device" errors even when disk capacity shows available space. Monitor this metric alongside disk space usage to ensure both storage capacity and file entry limits remain healthy.
panels.title: File Nodes Free

panels.description: This panel tracks the rate of disk I/O operations per second (IOPS) by displaying both read and write operations completed across all disk devices on the selected instance. The irate() function calculates the instantaneous per-second rate of change over a dynamically selected time window (based on Grafana's rate interval), providing a real-time view of disk activity rather than a long-term average. Each physical disk device is shown separately, allowing you to identify which specific disks are experiencing high I/O workloads. This metric measures the number of discrete I/O operations (such as random reads/writes) rather than throughput in bytes - a high IOPS count indicates the disk is handling many small operations, which is common with databases, virtual machines, or systems with many small files. Monitoring IOPS is essential for understanding disk performance bottlenecks, as even SSDs have limits on the number of operations they can handle per second. Sustained high IOPS combined with increased latency typically indicates the disk is reaching its performance limits and may require optimization, adding more disks, or migrating to faster storage.
panels.title: Disk IOps Completed

panels.description: This panel monitors system-wide file descriptor usage by comparing the number of currently allocated file descriptors against the system's maximum limit. File descriptors are handles used by the Linux kernel to manage access to files, sockets, pipes, and other I/O resources - every open file, network connection, or active process requires one or more file descriptors. The maximum limit (typically set via kernel parameters like fs.file-max) represents the total number of file descriptors the system can allocate, while the allocated count shows how many are currently in use across all processes. Monitoring these metrics together is critical because exhausting available file descriptors will cause applications to fail with "Too many open files" errors, preventing them from opening new files or establishing network connections even when other system resources are available. A consistently high ratio of allocated to maximum file descriptors may indicate file descriptor leaks in applications, insufficient system limits for the workload, or the need to tune kernel parameters to support higher concurrency.
panels.title: File Descriptors

panels.description: The rate of Redis errors by error type.
panels.title: Redis Error Rate

panels.description: This panel displays the top 10 Redis commands experiencing the highest failure rates across your instances. The query calculates the per-second rate of failed command executions over a 5-minute rolling window, then groups the results by both command type (GET, SET, HSET, etc.) and instance to show you exactly which operations are failing and where. By focusing on the current failure rate rather than cumulative totals, this panel helps you identify active problems that need immediate attention. High failure rates for specific commands typically indicate application bugs (incorrect data types, malformed requests), resource exhaustion (memory limits reached for SET operations), or infrastructure issues (network problems, authentication failures). Use this panel to prioritize troubleshooting efforts by addressing the most frequently failing commands first, and to determine whether failures are concentrated on a single instance (suggesting instance-specific problems) or distributed across your cluster (indicating application-level issues).
panels.title: Top 10 Failed Commands

panels.description: This panel tracks the rate at which Redis is rejecting incoming client connections on the selected instance. The query calculates the per-second rate of connection rejections over a 5-minute rolling window using the redis_rejected_connections_total counter metric. Connection rejections typically occur when Redis reaches its maxclients limit, meaning it has exhausted its available connection slots and cannot accept new clients. Any sustained rejection rate above zero is critical and indicates that applications are being denied access to Redis, which will cause application failures, timeouts, and degraded user experience. Common causes include insufficient maxclients configuration for your workload, connection leaks in application code where connections aren't properly closed, or a sudden spike in client connection attempts during traffic surges. When rejections are detected, immediately investigate current connection counts, review application connection pooling configurations, consider increasing the maxclients setting if you have available system resources, and audit your applications for connection management issues.
panels.title: Failed Connections

panels.description: Displays general memory values.
panels.title: Memory Usage Overview

panels.description: This shows how Redis memory is distributed between actual data (keys and values), Redis internal overhead (data structures, client buffers, replication buffers), and Lua script memory. It's important because it helps identify whether memory pressure is caused by too much data or excessive overhead, guiding optimization efforts. High overhead relative to dataset (>30%) suggests you have many small keys (high metadata-to-data ratio), large client output buffers from slow consumers, oversized replication backlog, or memory consumed by Lua scripts. Resolution involves consolidating small keys into larger data structures (use hashes instead of individual keys where possible), reviewing client buffer limits in redis.conf to prevent slow clients from consuming excessive memory, right-sizing the replication backlog (repl-backlog-size) based on actual replication lag patterns, optimizing Lua scripts to use less memory, and for BullMQ specifically, considering whether job data could be normalized or compressed to reduce per-job memory overhead.
panels.title: Memory Breakdown

panels.description: This metric compares the physical memory Redis is consuming (RSS - Resident Set Size) to the logical memory Redis has allocated for data. It's important for understanding true memory consumption versus what Redis thinks it's using. When RSS significantly exceeds allocated memory (high fragmentation), you're wasting physical RAM; when RSS is less than allocated (ratio <1.0), Redis is using compressed memory or swap, which severely degrades performance. Resolution for high RSS involves the defragmentation strategies mentioned above, while RSS below allocated memory is more concerning - it indicates Redis is swapping to disk or the OS is compressing memory, which causes severe latency. In the swap scenario, you must immediately free up system memory by stopping other services, increasing physical RAM, or reducing Redis's maxmemory limit; check `redis-cli INFO stats` for `used_memory_rss` and `used_memory` values, and monitor system-level swap usage with `free -h` and `vmstat`.
panels.title: RSS vs Allocated

panels.description: This composite metric includes fragmentation ratio, dataset percentage, overhead percentage, and peak vs current memory usage to provide a holistic view of memory health. It's important because these metrics together reveal whether Redis is using memory efficiently or experiencing issues. Poor efficiency (high overhead, high fragmentation, or significantly below peak) indicates memory management problems that will eventually cause performance issues or outages. Resolution involves the strategies mentioned above for fragmentation, plus monitoring peak memory to ensure your maxmemory setting has adequate headroom (configure maxmemory to 80% of physical RAM to leave room for spikes), investigating what caused historical peaks to prepare for future spikes, and reviewing BullMQ job processing patterns to smooth out memory usage spikes - for example, if jobs create large temporary data structures, consider processing them in smaller batches.
panels.title: Memory Efficiency

panels.description: This metric compares the physical memory Redis is using (RSS) to the logical memory Redis has allocated, calculated as RSS/allocated memory. It's critical for understanding memory efficiency because fragmentation means Redis is holding onto physical memory that's not actively storing data, which wastes resources and can lead to OOM conditions even when logical memory usage appears normal. A ratio above 1.5 indicates 50% memory waste due to fragmentation - memory freed by deleted keys hasn't been returned to the OS or reused efficiently, often caused by workload patterns where keys of varying sizes are created and deleted. Resolution involves restarting Redis during a maintenance window (which defragments by reloading from AOF/RDB with clean memory allocation), enabling active defragmentation in Redis 4.0+ with `CONFIG SET activedefrag yes`, tuning the allocator with `--enable-jemalloc` if you're using a different allocator, analyzing your data patterns to use more consistent key sizes, and if fragmentation correlates with AOF rewrites or high churn in BullMQ jobs, consider adjusting job retention policies to reduce the create/delete cycle rate.
panels.title: Fragmentation Ratio

panels.description: This is the absolute amount of wasted memory in megabytes due to fragmentation, calculated as RSS minus allocated memory. It's important because it quantifies exactly how much physical RAM is being wasted, helping you understand the real-world impact of fragmentation. High fragmented memory (>512MB) means you're wasting significant resources that could be used for actual data storage, causing Redis to consume more physical memory than necessary, which can lead to swapping or OOM kills. Resolution is similar to addressing fragmentation ratio - restart Redis to defragment, enable active defragmentation for gradual defragmentation without downtime, monitor memory patterns to identify which operations cause fragmentation spikes (like mass job deletions in BullMQ), consider adjusting your `maxmemory-policy` to more aggressively evict data if you're using Redis as a cache, and evaluate whether your BullMQ job data structures could be optimized to reduce memory churn.
panels.title: Fragmented Memory (MB)

panels.title: Redis Keys per DB

panels.description: This metric tracks keys forcibly removed by Redis due to memory pressure based on your eviction policy (likely `noeviction` in your setup). It's critical because evictions mean data loss - in your BullMQ environment, evicted keys could be job data, causing jobs to fail or be lost entirely. Any evictions (>0) indicate you've exceeded maxmemory and Redis is desperately removing data to make room, which should never happen in a queue system where all data is important. Resolution requires immediate investigation of memory usage to understand why you exceeded maxmemory, checking for unexpected spikes in job creation or large job payloads, verifying no memory leaks in application code, potentially increasing maxmemory if you have available physical RAM, implementing better job retention policies to remove completed/failed jobs more aggressively with BullMQ's built-in cleanup, considering whether some job data could be stored elsewhere (database) with only references in Redis, and if using Redis for both cache and queue, separating them into dedicated instances with appropriate eviction policies.
panels.title: Key Evictions

panels.description: This metric tracks keys that are removed when their TTL (Time To Live) expires. This is normal and expected behavior for cache and session data.
panels.title: Key Expirations

panels.description:
Successful key lookups per second over a 5 minute window. Commands that trigger hits:

- GET (key exists)
- MGET (each existing key counts)
- EXISTS (key exists)
- GETSET (key exists)
panels.title: Keyspace Hits

panels.description:
The number of failed key lookups per second over a 5 minute window. Commands that trigger misses:

- GET (key doesn't exist)
- MGET (each missing key counts)
- EXISTS (key doesn't exist)
- Any read operation that doesn't find the key
panels.title: Keyspace Misses

panels.description: The top 10 commands per second by type over a 5 minute window.
panels.title: Top 10 Commands

panels.description: This measures the total number of commands Redis processes per second across all command types. It's important as the primary indicator of Redis workload and activity level, showing how busy your instance is. High throughput (>50k commands/sec) indicates Redis is handling significant load, which is expected in production but should be monitored against baseline to detect anomalies. Extreme throughput (>100k/sec) can approach Redis's capacity limits, risking latency increases and performance degradation. Resolution involves understanding your baseline throughput to identify unusual spikes, investigating correlation with application changes or traffic patterns, using `SLOWLOG GET` to identify expensive commands consuming resources, optimizing application code to reduce unnecessary Redis calls (batch operations, pipeline commands, cache results).
panels.title: Total Command Throughput

panels.description: The percentage of top 20 redis cmds used during the last 5 minutes.
panels.title: Command Distribution

panels.description: This measures the average time taken to execute commands, calculated as total execution time divided by total commands. It's critical for performance because high latency directly translates to slow application response times and poor user experience. Elevated latency (>1ms average) indicates Redis is struggling to keep up with load, blocked by slow operations, experiencing resource contention (CPU, memory, or I/O), or affected by network issues. Resolution requires identifying slow commands with `SLOWLOG GET` to find operations taking excessive time, checking for blocking operations like KEYS, SORT without LIMIT, or operations on very large keys (millions of elements in sets/lists), reviewing CPU and memory usage to ensure Redis has adequate resources, investigating whether slow disk I/O during AOF writes or RDB saves is causing latency spikes, optimizing application code to avoid expensive operations or use them less frequently, considering whether background persistence operations (AOF rewrites) should be scheduled differently, and potentially splitting workload across multiple Redis instances if latency persists despite optimization.
panels.title: Average Command Latency

panels.description: This boolean metric indicates whether Append-Only File persistence is enabled, which logs every write operation to disk for durability. It's critical for data persistence because without AOF (or RDB snapshots), Redis only keeps data in memory, and you'll lose all data on restart or crash - unacceptable for your BullMQ job queue. Having AOF disabled means any crash results in complete job loss, making your job processing system unreliable. Resolution requires enabling AOF by setting `appendonly yes` in redis.conf and restarting Redis, or dynamically with `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` followed by `CONFIG REWRITE` to persist the change, understanding this will cause an immediate fork to create the initial AOF file (brief CPU spike), and verifying you have adequate disk space for the AOF file (typically 1-2x your dataset size plus growth room).
panels.title: AOF Enabled?

panels.description: This composite metric checks for delayed fsync operations, which occur when Redis cannot sync writes to disk fast enough. It's critical because delayed fsyncs mean write operations are sitting in memory buffers without being written to disk, creating a data loss risk if Redis crashes before the flush completes. Unhealthy AOF (delayed fsync >0) indicates your disk is too slow to keep up with write volume, you're experiencing I/O contention from other processes, the disk is failing, or you're hitting storage system limits (especially in cloud environments with provisioned IOPS). Resolution requires immediate investigation of disk I/O with `iostat -x 1` to check for saturation, reviewing what other processes are consuming disk I/O (`iotop`), verifying disk health with SMART data or cloud monitoring, considering switching to faster storage (NVMe vs SSD vs HDD), reducing Redis write volume if possible (review BullMQ job creation rate), changing `appendfsync` from `always` to `everysec` if you're using the former (trades 1 second of potential data loss for better performance), or in cloud environments, increasing provisioned IOPS for your storage volumes.
panels.title: AOF Health

panels.description: This specific metric counts pending fsync operations waiting to be written to disk. It's critical as the primary indicator of persistence problems that lead to data loss. Any value >0 is concerning because it means Redis has queued write operations that haven't reached disk yet, directly violating your zero-data-loss requirement. Resolution is similar to AOF health above, with additional emphasis on immediate action - this is a data loss emergency requiring urgent investigation of disk performance, potential temporary reduction of write load by throttling BullMQ job creation, verification that you haven't run out of disk space (`df -h`), checking for filesystem errors (`dmesg | grep -i error`), and if this occurs during AOF rewrite, considering increasing `aof-rewrite-incremental-fsync yes` to spread out the I/O load, or scheduling rewrites during low-traffic periods.
panels.title: Delayed AOF Writes

panels.description: This metric tracks how long the last AOF rewrite took to complete. It's important because AOF rewrites are fork operations that briefly pause Redis, create CPU spikes, and can cause replication lag if they take too long. Long rewrites (>5 minutes) indicate large datasets taking time to write, slow disk I/O, or insufficient system resources during the rewrite process, which can cause replicas to fall behind and potentially require full resyncs. Resolution involves monitoring rewrite duration trends over time to understand if it's growing with your dataset, ensuring rewrites occur during low-traffic periods by tuning `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage` and `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size`, enabling `aof-rewrite-incremental-fsync` yes to prevent I/O spikes, verifying you have adequate free memory for the fork (child process temporarily doubles memory usage), considering faster storage, and if rewrites consistently cause issues, evaluating whether you could use RDB snapshots instead or reduce AOF file growth by cleaning up old BullMQ jobs more aggressively.
panels.title: Rewrite Duration

panels.description: This metric shows the number of background I/O operations waiting to sync AOF data to disk. It's important as a real-time indicator of persistence backlog, showing whether your disk can keep pace with writes. High pending data (>10) indicates sustained I/O pressure where writes are arriving faster than they can be persisted, signaling disk saturation or impending AOF delay issues. Resolution involves the same disk performance investigations as delayed AOF writes, plus proactive measures like monitoring disk queue depth and I/O utilization to catch issues before they become critical, implementing write throttling in your application layer if necessary, reviewing whether you can optimize BullMQ job payloads to reduce write volume (compress job data, reduce job metadata), and considering whether some job data could be stored elsewhere (like a database) with only references in Redis.
panels.title: Pending AOF data

panels.description: This boolean indicates whether Redis is currently performing an AOF rewrite operation. It's important as a diagnostic indicator because rewrites consume significant CPU, memory (fork), and I/O resources, which can explain temporary performance degradation. When this is true (1) and you're experiencing performance issues, the rewrite is the likely culprit - it's a fork operation that copies memory, intensively writes to disk, and can cause replication lag as replicas wait for the master. Resolution isn't typically needed as this is normal operation, but if rewrites consistently cause problems, you should tune rewrite thresholds to make them less frequent (`auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 200` instead of 100), schedule them during maintenance windows using manual `BGREWRITEAOF` commands instead of automatic triggers, ensure adequate system resources (especially free memory for the fork), monitor the duration to ensure they complete reasonably quickly, and alert if they take exceptionally long as that indicates deeper issues.
panels.title: AOF Rewrite in progress?

panels.description: This metric measures how many seconds behind the master each replica is based on replication stream timing. It's critical for failover safety because high lag means the replica doesn't have recent data, and promoting it would cause data loss. Lag >10 seconds means the replica can't keep up with the master's write rate due to network latency, replica being overloaded (CPU/disk), replica processing slow commands, or network partition reducing throughput. Resolution requires identifying which replica is lagging using `redis-cli INFO replication` on the master, checking replica CPU/memory/disk usage for resource constraints, verifying network connectivity and bandwidth between master and replica with `iperf`, reviewing replica logs for slow operations or errors, ensuring the replica has adequate hardware (replicas should match master specs), checking if the replication backlog is sized appropriately (`repl-backlog-size` should handle expected lag), and investigating whether master write volume has increased beyond replica's capacity to replicate (may need to reduce write rate or optimize replica performance).
panels.title: Replica Lag

panels.description: This metric measures the byte offset difference between the master's replication position and each replica's position. It's important because it quantifies exactly how much data the replica is behind, helping assess data loss risk during failover. Large byte lag (>10MB) indicates sustained replication delay where replicas are falling progressively further behind, risking a full resync if the gap exceeds the replication backlog size. Resolution involves the same approaches as time-based lag (check replica resources, network, etc.), but also specifically reviewing the replication backlog size - if byte lag approaches `repl-backlog-size`, you need to increase it immediately with `CONFIG SET repl-backlog-size 256mb` to prevent full resyncs, considering temporarily reducing master write rate if replicas can't catch up, monitoring whether lag correlates with AOF rewrites or other background operations on replicas, and ensuring replicas aren't processing expensive read operations that compete with replication processing.
panels.title: Replica Lag (bytes)

panels.description: File size and growth rate of the AOF file.
panels.title: AOF File Stats

panels.description: This metric calculates the rate at which your AOF file is growing over time. It's important for capacity planning and understanding write patterns, helping predict when you'll need more disk space or when rewrites will trigger. Rapid growth (>100MB/hour) indicates high write volume to Redis, which is expected in busy BullMQ environments but should be monitored for unexpected spikes. Resolution involves verifying the growth rate matches your expected job processing volume, investigating spikes that correlate with application changes or traffic patterns, ensuring disk space grows proportionally with AOF growth, reviewing whether job data could be reduced (compress payloads, minimize metadata), considering whether job retention policies are appropriately cleaning up completed jobs, and if growth is unsustainable, evaluating architectural changes like storing job results elsewhere or using Redis more sparingly for job state.
panels.title: AOF File Growth

panels.description: This counts failed authentication attempts against Redis. It's critical for security because authentication failures indicate someone is trying to access Redis with incorrect credentials, which could be a brute force attack, misconfigured application, or unauthorized access attempt. Any authentication failures should be investigated immediately as they represent security threats or configuration errors. Resolution requires identifying the source of failed attempts using `CLIENT LIST` and reviewing logs for source IPs, determining if it's a legitimate application with wrong credentials (fix configuration), an attacker attempting unauthorized access (block IP, review firewall rules), or a compromised credential (immediately rotate passwords), ensuring all applications use correct passwords (check connection strings in BullMQ and Itential configurations), implementing network-level restrictions to limit Redis access to known application servers only, considering disabling password authentication in favor of certificate-based auth or cloud provider IAM if available, and monitoring for patterns of attacks to implement additional security measures.
panels.title: Auth Failures

panels.description: This counts commands rejected because the authenticated user doesn't have permission to execute them. It's important for security and operational health because command violations indicate misconfigured ACLs or applications trying to run commands they shouldn't. Violations suggest your ACL rules are too restrictive (legitimate applications can't do their job), you've assigned wrong ACL profiles to users, or something is trying to run privileged commands like CONFIG, SHUTDOWN, or FLUSHALL. Resolution involves reviewing the rejected commands using Redis logs to understand what's being blocked, checking which user/client is being denied with `ACL GETUSER` username, determining if the application legitimately needs that command (adjust ACL rules with `ACL SETUSER`), or if it's attempting operations it shouldn't (fix application code or investigate if it's compromised), ensuring BullMQ workers have appropriate permissions for their operations (typically need read/write on specific keys, pub/sub for events), and maintaining principle of least privilege by only granting necessary commands to each application.
panels.title: Command Failures

panels.description: This tracks attempts to access keys that the authenticated user doesn't have permission to read/write. It's important for data security and multi-tenancy, ensuring applications can only access their designated data. Violations indicate ACL key patterns are too restrictive, applications are trying to access wrong key namespaces, or there's a security issue where one application is trying to access another's data. Resolution requires identifying which keys are being denied access through Redis logs, reviewing the key patterns in ACL rules (`ACL GETUSER username` shows allowed patterns), determining if the application should have access (modify ACL with `ACL SETUSER username ~newpattern:*`), or if it's a bug causing the app to request wrong keys (fix application logic), ensuring your BullMQ queues and jobs use consistent key naming that matches ACL patterns (like bull:myqueue:*), and if you're running multiple applications or tenants, verifying they're properly isolated with non-overlapping key patterns.
panels.title: Key Access Failures

panels.description: This counts pub/sub channel access denials. It's important for systems using Redis pub/sub, which BullMQ uses extensively for job events and worker coordination. Violations indicate applications can't subscribe to or publish on necessary channels, breaking event-driven communication. Channel denials mean ACL rules don't include required channel patterns for pub/sub, BullMQ workers can't receive job notifications, or applications are trying to use wrong channel names. Resolution involves identifying which channels are being blocked in Redis logs, reviewing ACL channel patterns (`ACL GETUSER username` shows `&channel:*` patterns), understanding BullMQ's channel naming (typically `bull:queuename:events`), adjusting ACL rules to allow required channels with `ACL SETUSER username &bull:*:*`, verifying BullMQ configuration uses expected channel names, and ensuring workers have pub/sub permissions for both publishing job results and subscribing to job notifications.
panels.title: Channel Failures

panels.description: This measures bytes per second moving in/out of Redis over the network, showing input (client commands), output (responses), and total bandwidth consumption. It's important for capacity planning and understanding replication overhead - high throughput indicates significant data movement, which can saturate network links or indicate inefficiently large payloads. High network usage (>500MB/s) suggests you're moving substantial data, which is fine if your network can handle it, but approaching network limits (900MB/s on a 1Gbps link) risks saturation that will cause performance degradation. Resolution involves monitoring baseline throughput to identify anomalies, investigating spikes that might indicate large keys being retrieved or excessive replication traffic, optimizing application code to reduce payload sizes (compress job data in BullMQ, avoid storing unnecessary metadata), reviewing whether you're retrieving large keys that could be split into smaller pieces, checking if replication is consuming excessive bandwidth (large datasets, frequent AOF rewrites), considering network upgrades if legitimate usage exceeds capacity, and potentially implementing compression at the application layer to reduce network transfer volume.
